assessment.title: Homework #4 · MOSFET device operation
assessment.topic: Module 4 · MOSFET · Triode resistance · Saturation · Device sizing
assessment.instructions: Show key steps, assumptions, and final answers with units. Use the square-law model: triode with small v_DS, r_DS = 1/[k_n′(W/L)V_OV]; saturation, I_D = ½k_n′(W/L)V_OV² for V_DS ≥ V_OV, with k_n′ = μ_nC_ox and V_OV = V_GS − V_t. State and check the operating region. Enter numbers in the units shown.

questions.title: 1) Triode resistance r_DS: scaling factors
questions.promptHtml:
An NMOS transistor operated with a small vDS exhibits a resistance rDS. By what factor will rDS change in each situation?

  1. VOV is doubled.
  2. The device is replaced by one in the same technology with double the width.
  3. The device is replaced by one in the same technology with both width and length doubled.
  4. The device is replaced by one in a more advanced technology with the oxide thickness halved, and W and L scaled similarly (halved).

Enter each answer as the ratio rDS,new/rDS,old.
hints: For small v_DS: r_DS = 1/[k_n′(W/L)V_OV] with k_n′ = μ_nC_ox.
C_ox = ε_ox/t_ox, so halving t_ox doubles k_n′.
checklist: Write r_DS in terms of k_n′, W/L and V_OV.
Identify which factor changes in each case.

responseFields.label: (c) Factor for W and L doubled
(d) Factor for t_ox, W, L halved
Explain each result from the r_DS expression

questions.title: 2) NMOS as a variable resistor (200 Ω to 1 kΩ)
questions.promptHtml: An NMOS transistor in a technology with kn′ = 400 μA/V2 and Vt = 0.4 V operates with small vDS as a variable resistor ranging from 200 Ω to 1 kΩ. Specify the range required for the control voltage VGS and the required transistor width W. Use the smallest possible device, as limited by the minimum channel length Lmin = 0.18 μm and the maximum allowed voltage of 1.8 V.
hints: The smallest resistance needs the largest V_OV: V_GS = 1.8 V → V_OV = 1.4 V.
r_DS ∝ 1/V_OV, so 1 kΩ needs one-fifth of that overdrive.
checklist: Size W/L for 200 Ω at V_GS = 1.8 V.

questions.title: 3) Width for a 1 kΩ minimum resistance
questions.promptHtml: An n-channel MOS device in a technology with oxide thickness 20 nm, minimum channel length 1 μm, kn′ = 100 μA/V2, and Vt = 0.8 V operates in the triode region with small vDS and with VGS in the range 0 V to +5 V. What device width is needed to ensure that the minimum available resistance is 1 kΩ?
hints: The minimum resistance occurs at the maximum V_GS = 5 V.
Use L = L_min = 1 μm; t_ox is not needed because k_n′ is given.

questions.promptHtml:
A CMOS process has Lmin = 0.25 μm, tox = 6 nm, μn = 460 cm2/V·s, and Vt = 0.5 V.

  2. For an NMOS transistor with W/L = 15 μm/0.25 μm, calculate VOV, VGS, and VDS,min needed to operate in saturation with a dc current ID = 0.8 mA.
  3. For the same device, find VOV and VGS required to operate it as a 500 Ω resistor for very small vDS.

Use εox = 3.9ε0 = 3.45×10−11 F/m.
hints: Saturation: I_D = ½k_n′(W/L)V_OV². Triode (small v_DS): r_DS = 1/[k_n′(W/L)V_OV].
checklist: Compute C_ox and k_n′ with consistent units.
Solve the saturation equation for V_OV.
Solve the triode resistance for V_OV.

A particular n-channel enhancement MOSFET is measured to have a drain current of 0.4 mA at VGS = VDS = 2 V and of 0.1 mA at VGS = VDS = 1.5 V. What are the values of kn and Vt for this device?

Use ID = ½kn(VGS − Vt)2 with kn = kn′(W/L).
hints: With V_DS = V_GS > V_GS − V_t the device is always in saturation.
Take the ratio of the two currents so k_n cancels.
checklist: Use the current ratio to find V_t.

questions.title: 9) Circuit Studio · Extract k_n and V_t, then look inside the channel (the Lab 7 method)
questions.promptHtml:
Circuit Studio problem · DC values, Simulate I–V curves and Inside the device lens. Simulation tools are switched on for this question. Record each prediction before you use the tool that checks it.

The NMOS is driven by a gate source VG and a drain source VDS. Its parameters are not printed on the drawing: treat Circuit Studio as your bench, as you will the real transistor in Lab 7.

  1. With VDS = 3 V, set VG = 1.0 V and click Show values; record ID. Repeat with VG = 1.5 V.
  2. Extract Vt and kn from the two points using ID = ½kn(VGS − Vt)². Check them against the Modelling notes in the values panel.
  3. Open Simulate → I–V curves, click Run, and confirm the Q-point lies on the curve for VGS = 1.5 V.
  4. With VG = 1.5 V, open Visual Aids ▾ → Inside the device and click M1. Record what the lens shows for the channel at VDS = 3 V, then at VDS = 0.3 V. Predict ID at 0.3 V from your extracted parameters before you read it.
  5. Explain: why the channel shape changes between the two VDS values, and why the Vt and kn you measure on a real part in Lab 7 will differ from part to part.
